title: The ABC's of Who Benefits from Working with AI: Ability, Beliefs, and Calibration
author: Andrew Caplin · David J. Deming · Shangwen Li · Daniel J. Martin · Philip Marx · Ben Weidmann · Kadachi Jiada Ye

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source presents a controlled comparison of human judgments with and without calibrated AI assistance, consistent with the cluster’s emphasis on testing human–AI performance rather than inferring benefits from capability alone. However, the supplied evidence contains only methods and descriptive statistics, with no outcome findings on time, quality, learning, verification costs or who actually benefits, so its substantive position on practical productivity cannot be determined.
qs: Our aim was to select 160 images from this dataset so that the distribution of probability reports would be as even as possible, which would provide room for both humans and the AI to contribute in helping to identify the category of an image.

It provides experimental evidence that benefits vary with participants’ awareness of their own ability, with well-calibrated, lower-ability participants gaining most, while keeping the larger inequality reduction from eliminating miscalibration explicitly counterfactual.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s claim that AI gains depend on user capability rather than access alone, and materially extends it by identifying accurate self-assessment (calibration) as a measurable mechanism shaping who benefits. It also proposes calibration training as an organisational complement, while its non-legal, bounded prediction task limits direct generalisation to legal workflows.
qs: However, holding ability constant, AI assistance is more valuable for people who are calibrated, meaning they have accurate beliefs about their own ability.
In domains where direct upskilling is costly or time consuming, our results suggest that the combination of calibration training and AI assistance may be particularly valuable.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts that AI gains are heterogeneous and materially extends the cluster by identifying accurate self-assessment as a mechanism shaping who benefits. Its experiment finds the largest gains among low-ability but well-calibrated users, while showing that miscalibration can prevent weaker users from capturing the greatest benefits.
qs: Second, we find that participants with high calibration and low ability gain the most from working with AI.
Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s account of heterogeneous, user-dependent gains and materially extends it by experimentally identifying belief calibration—distinct from baseline ability—as a predictor of who benefits from AI assistance. Its findings refine the cluster’s emphasis on user expertise and interaction quality, showing that lower-ability users may gain substantially when well calibrated, while miscalibration can produce harmful reliance errors.
qs: Our main prediction is that conditional on their individual ability Ai , individuals who are more calibrated will benefit more from working with AI in terms of their AI-augmented ability Āi .
A one standard deviation increase in calibration in- crease the impact of AI assistance by 1.4 percentage points, or about 20 percent of the total treatment e↵ect of 6.9 percentage points.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that AI assistance can improve a specific task without producing uniform gains across participants. It reports higher image-identification accuracy overall, while treatment effects vary negatively with baseline accuracy and IQ and positively with calibration, reinforcing the need to distinguish among skill measures.
qs: Column 1 shows the impact of AI assistance on accuracy in a simple bivariation regression.9 AI improves participants’ ability to accurately identify an image by 6.9 percentage points, an increase of more than 10 percent relative to the control mean of 65.5 percent.

st.t: Human-AI decisions: Self-knowledge conditions unrealized gains
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central claim that AI-assistance gains are conditional rather than automatic: average accuracy improves, but the size of the benefit depends materially on users’ calibration about their own ability. Its counterfactual further supports the claim of unrealized gains by estimating that miscalibration limits AI’s equalising effect, though it does not address case-level model error or test workflow interventions.
qs: Holding baseline ability fixed, a one standard deviation increase in calibration increases the average treatment e↵ect of AI assistance by 20 percent.

In a counterfactual analysis where miscalibration is eliminated, the productivity gap (captured by interquartile ratio, a measure of spread) would shrink nearly twice as much as it does already with the introduction of AI assistance.

kp.k: Experiment separates baseline ability from belief calibration
kp.d: The authors study AI-assisted age classification rather than legal work. They recruited 732 U.S.-resident participants through Prolific across two sessions: 493 were assigned to receive AI assistance and 239 to never receive it. Participants assessed 160 photographs, reporting the probability that each person was over 21. Treated participants received AI predictions for 80 images; unassisted blocks supplied baseline ability and calibration measures. A 14-question Raven’s Progressive Matrices task measured general cognitive ability. The October 2024 working paper had not been peer-reviewed.
qs: We ask 732 experimental participants to report the likelihood that 160 di↵erent people in photographs are over 21 years of age.
Of those, 493 were assigned to the treatment of working with AI, and 239 were assigned to the control of never working with the AI.
They have not been peer-reviewed or been subject to the review by the NBER Board of Directors that accompanies official NBER publications.

kp.k: Calibration concerns knowing one's own predictive reliability
kp.d: Ability is measured as expected classification accuracy using a 50% decision threshold. The main calibration measure is the negative absolute difference between average confidence and average correctness, distinguishing accurate self-assessment from high confidence or high ability. The authors condition on ability because calibration is mechanically related to accuracy. Their task and image selection were designed to provide clear ground truth, suitable difficulty and calibrated AI predictions.
qs: We use the relationship between an individual’s beliefs Bi and the true states S to define a simple measure of both the individual’s ability – what they know – and calibration – how well they know what they know.
In either case, the larger the di↵erence between perceived and actual performance, the less an individual’s beliefs are calibrated.

kp.k: AI increases accuracy, especially for lower-ability participants
kp.d: Randomized AI assistance increased classification accuracy by 6.9 percentage points, more than 10% relative to the control mean of 65.5%. In the specification adding baseline accuracy and its treatment interaction, a one-standard-deviation increase in accuracy reduced the assistance benefit by 1.6 percentage points. Lower Raven’s-test performers also benefited more when that measure was included. These are findings about prediction accuracy in the experimental task, not measured changes in legal productivity or employment.
qs: AI improves participants’ ability to accurately identify an image by 6.9 percentage points, an increase of more than 10 percent relative to the control mean of 65.5 percent.
a one standard deviation increase in accuracy decreases the impact of AI assistance by 1.6 percentage points.
Similar to the accuracy measure, we find that low IQ participants benefit more from AI help.

kp.k: Better-calibrated participants obtain larger AI benefits
kp.d: Holding baseline ability constant, a one-standard-deviation increase in calibration increased AI’s benefit by approximately 1.4 percentage points, about 20% of the overall 6.9-percentage-point treatment effect. The accuracy and calibration interactions were statistically significant below the 5% level; adding the cognitive-ability measure did not meaningfully change the calibration coefficients. Linear projections for hypothetical participants one standard deviation above or below mean ability and calibration put the largest gain—nearly 10 percentage points—among low-ability, well-calibrated participants, and the smallest among high-accuracy, miscalibrated participants.
qs: Unlike the interaction with accuracy, we find that better-calibrated participants benefit more from AI assistance.
Both interaction terms are statistically significant at the less than five percent level.
Participants with low ability but accurate beliefs benefit the most – nearly 10 percentage points – from AI assistance.
By contrast, participants with high accuracy but miscalibrated beliefs benefit the least.

kp.k: Human discretion often falls short of AI alone
kp.d: The AI ranked in the top 6% of unaided human performers, although participants were informed only that it was better than the average human and worse than the best. Despite average improvement with assistance, 68% of treated participants performed worse than if they had followed the AI recommendations wholesale. Among humans working alone, 79.5% were overconfident, with confidence exceeding accuracy by 10.6 percentage points on average. Participants matched the AI recommendation within one percentage point only 6% of the time with assistance, versus 2% without it.
qs: First, the AI has ability in the top 6% of human performers working alone, and working with the AI significantly improves average human performance in our task.
with 68% of treated subjects still performing worse than if they had followed the AI recommendations wholesale.
Subjects repeat the AI recommendation exactly (i.e., within a percentage point) 6% of the time with AI and 2% of the time without AI.

kp.k: Confidence affects when people defer to AI
kp.d: The authors propose that underconfidence can cause excessive reliance on incorrect AI predictions, while overconfidence can cause rejection of correct predictions. Their analysis replacing calibration with net confidence and separating images by whether the AI was correct supports this mechanism: less-confident participants were relatively more disadvantaged when AI was wrong, and more-confident participants when AI was right. The introductory argument presents calibration as important across different levels of AI capability, rather than treating either greater confidence or greater deference as universally beneficial.
qs: If the AI’s prediction is very poor, under-confident workers will defer too much even if they have better information.

Under- confident participants may commit too many Type I errors (following the AI when it is incorrect), while over-confident individuals may commit too many Type II errors (failing to follow the AI when it is correct).

kp.k: Robustness checks address measurement and specification concerns
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that measurement error in ability could generate a spurious calibration effect in a multivariate regression. They report that calibration alone did not significantly predict performance among controls, and an adaptation of Obviously Related Instrumental Variables produced larger, less precise calibration effects that remained statistically significant. They also report similar results with demographic controls and replicate the main findings using AUC for ability and an alternative calibration measure based on Grether’s functional form.
qs: the co- efficient on standardized calibration alone is economically and statistically insignificant across specifications in Table 1.
Table 3 replicates the main results but with demographic controls. We find very similar results.
We replicate our main findings.

kp.k: Perfect calibration could amplify performance equalization
kp.d: In a regression-based counterfactual, the interquartile range of predicted performance fell from 5.84 without AI to 3.86 with AI under observed calibration, a 34% reduction. Setting everyone’s confidence equal to accuracy yielded an IQR of 5.80 without assistance and 2.30 with assistance, a 61% reduction relative to the original baseline—an additional 27 percentage points. The authors attribute this difference to lower-ability participants also tending to be less calibrated. These are simulated performance-distribution results, not experimentally demonstrated effects of calibration training or estimates of wage inequality. The results section uses interquartile range, although the introduction calls the spread measure an interquartile ratio.
qs: We estimate an IQR of 5.84 when participants work without AI, compared to an IQR of 3.86 with AI, representing a 34% reduction in performance inequality from AI assistance.
However, with AI assistance, perfect calibration reduces the IQR to 2.30, which represents a 61% reduction in performance inequality relative to baseline (Scenario 1).
This is because of the joint distribution of ability and calibration: the low-ability individuals who stand to gain the most from working with AI are also among the least calibrated.

kp.k: Calibration training is promising but remains untested here
kp.d: The authors suggest combining calibration training with AI assistance, especially where direct skill development is costly or slow. They cite prior studies reporting improvements in calibration, including short interventions lasting less than an hour, but their own experiment did not test such training. Whether calibration can be trained for collaborative AI work, how to do so and who benefits are explicitly left to future research.
qs: A natural set of questions that we leave to future work is if, how, and for whom individual calibration can be trained as a skill for the collaborative nature of work with AI.

Among the characteristics that we show are related to performance when working with AI (baseline skill, IQ, and calibration), calibration appears to be a relatively strong candidate for policy and training.
In domains where direct upskilling is costly or time consuming, our results suggest that the combination of calibration training and AI assistance may be particularly valuable.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Caplin and co-authors find that AI improves age-classification accuracy, with larger benefits for lower-ability participants and, holding ability constant, better-calibrated participants.
pts.d: The authors report an average accuracy gain of 6.9 percentage points relative to a control mean of 65.5%. A one-standard-deviation increase in calibration is associated with approximately 1.4 percentage points more benefit from AI, about 20% of the average treatment effect. Low-ability participants with well-calibrated beliefs gain the most: nearly 10 percentage points in the authors’ projections for hypothetical skill-calibration groups. These are claims about AI-assisted probabilistic classification, not findings about legal services.

pts.k: AI assistance does not eliminate differences in human performance or guarantee that human–AI combinations outperform AI alone.
pts.d: The authors report that the AI ranked in the top 6% of unaided human performers, yet 68% of assisted participants performed worse than they would have by following its recommendations wholesale. They describe different risks of miscalibration: underconfident participants may follow incorrect AI advice, while overconfident participants may reject correct advice. Their analysis disaggregating performance by whether AI predictions were correct supports this account of differential reliance.

pts.k: The authors estimate that AI reduces performance inequality and predict substantially greater equalisation if miscalibration were eliminated.
pts.d: Their regression-based exercise estimates that AI reduces the interquartile range of predicted performance from 5.84 to 3.86, a 34% reduction. Under simulated perfect calibration, AI-assisted performance has an interquartile range of 2.30, a 61% reduction relative to the original unaided baseline. Thus, eliminating miscalibration is predicted to add 27 percentage points to the inequality reduction. This is a counterfactual about task performance, not an observed calibration-training effect or a finding about wages or employment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is a controlled experiment with 732 participants; calibration-training benefits are proposed rather than tested.
pts.d: The October 2024 NBER working paper reports two experimental sessions with US-resident adults recruited through Prolific. Participants assessed 160 facial photographs; 493 were assigned AI assistance for half the rounds and 239 never received assistance. Unaided rounds supplied baseline ability and calibration measures. The AI used the Caffe age-prediction model described by Rothe and colleagues. The authors report robustness checks using demographic controls, measurement-error adjustments and alternative ability and calibration measures. AI assistance was randomly assigned, but calibration was measured rather than experimentally manipulated. The perfect-calibration results are model-based counterfactuals. Prior calibration-training studies motivate the proposed intervention. The paper states that it had not been peer-reviewed.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings concern immediate assistance in a deliberately controlled classification task; broader workplace and training implications have no specified implementation horizon.
pts.d: The experiment measures within-session accuracy rather than long-term learning or labour-market outcomes. The task had objective age labels, required no specialist training and used selected images to make AI predictions calibrated and more accurate than the average participant but less accurate than the best. Participants were informed of these properties and received no outcome feedback during the incentivised rounds. The authors suggest calibration training combined with AI may be especially valuable where direct upskilling is costly or slow, but leave whether, how and for whom such training works to future research.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is non-specialist adult participants; the authors’ wider implications concern workers using AI decision support.
pts.d: Lower-baseline-ability participants gain more on average, especially when they accurately assess their own ability. Higher-accuracy but miscalibrated participants gain least in the authors’ projected groups. Lower Raven’s-test scorers also gain more, without materially changing the calibration relationship. Because low-ability participants tend to be less calibrated, those with the greatest potential gains may not fully realise them. The source does not establish effects on lawyers, firms, clients, legal prices or access to justice; its legal-work reference is contextual literature rather than its own legal-domain evidence.
